nameStory: The 'bachelor's button' name comes from an old European tradition where young men would wear these button-like flowers in their lapels, with the belief that the flower's condition would reveal their romantic fate. This particular species earned the 'Brazilian' prefix because it's native to South America, distinguishing it from the more familiar cornflower that shares the bachelor's button name.
description: Brazilian bachelor's button is a small flowering plant in the sunflower family that's extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in the region. It produces small, purple to violet flower heads that look like tiny pincushions or buttons. This low-growing plant typically reaches about 1-2 feet tall and has a somewhat weedy appearance with simple leaves arranged alternately along the stems.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, button-like purple to violet flower heads about the size of a dime, composed entirely of tiny disc flowers with no surrounding petals, giving them a fuzzy, pincushion appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Simple, oval to lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly rough to the touch, arranged alternately along the stem with visible veins

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing, somewhat sprawling plant that forms small clumps, typically staying under 2 feet tall with multiple branching stems

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry seeds with tiny bristles or scales that help them disperse in the wind, typical of the sunflower family

habitat: Given its extreme rarity in New England with only one observation, its preferred habitat here is unclear. In its native range, it typically grows in disturbed soils, waste areas, and along roadsides. If found in New England, it would likely be in similar disturbed sites, possibly as an accidental introduction near ports or botanical gardens.

seasonality.spring: Young plants may emerge from seed, but flowering typically doesn't begin this early in the season.
seasonality.summer: Primary flowering period when the distinctive purple button-like flower heads are most visible and diagnostic.
seasonality.fall: Late flowers may still be present early in the season, and seeds are developing and dispersing.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely, leaving no above-ground parts for identification.

funFact: This plant is so rare in New England that botanists have recorded it only once in the entire region, making it one of the most elusive members of the sunflower family you could possibly encounter on a nature walk!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small purple flowers in the aster family, but the distinctive button-like appearance with no surrounding ray petals (the white 'petals' you see on daisies) sets it apart from most common New England wildflowers.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with the common cornflower (Centaurea cyanus), which is also called bachelor's button but is blue and much more common in New England gardens and roadsides. They're in different genera despite sharing a common name.
compareHints: Since it's the only Centratherum species in our region, compare it to other small purple flowers in the sunflower family like New England asters or ironweeds. Unlike these relatives, Brazilian bachelor's button has no ray petals around its flower heads and maintains a much smaller, more compact growth form.
